record.paper_title: Open problems on graphs arising from geometric topology
record.original_question: Let K be a tree embedded in R^2 and let epsilon be positive. An epsilon-triod is a plane triod made from three arcs meeting only at one common point, with each arm containing a point whose distance from the union of the other two arms is greater than epsilon. A tree is epsilon-narrow if some arc I contained in K has every point of K within distance epsilon of I. A tree is epsilon-spanned if two non-intersecting closed disks of diameter epsilon with centers constrained to move on K cannot move so that their traces on K are the same. Prove or disprove the two narrowness assertions: every plane tree with no epsilon-triods is 10 epsilon-narrow, and every epsilon-spanned plane tree is 10 epsilon-narrow.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Work in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. A plane tree is a topological tree (a compact, connected, locally connected, 1-dimensional space with no simple closed curves) embedded in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a plane tree.

Define the following three notions.

(1) An $\varepsilon$-triod in $K$ is a subset $T \subset K$ that is the union of three arcs $A_1, A_2, A_3$ meeting only at one common endpoint $v$, such that each $A_i$ contains a point whose distance from $A_j \cup A_k$ (where $\{i,j,k\} = \{1,2,3\}$) is greater than $\varepsilon$.

(2) $K$ is $\varepsilon$-narrow if there exists an arc $I \subset K$ such that every point of $K$ lies within Euclidean distance $\varepsilon$ of $I$.

(3) $K$ is $\varepsilon$-spanned if there do not exist two continuous motions of closed disks $D_1(t), D_2(t)$ of diameter $\varepsilon$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, whose centers are constrained to lie on $K$, such that $D_1(t) \cap D_2(t) = \emptyset$ for all $t$ and such that $\{D_1(t) \cap K : t\} = \{D_2(t) \cap K : t\}$ as families of subsets of $K$ (i.e., the disks cannot be moved along $K$, while remaining disjoint, in such a way that they trace out the same set on $K$).

Prove or disprove the following two assertions:

(a) Every plane tree $K$ that contains no $\varepsilon$-triod is $10\varepsilon$-narrow.

(b) Every $\varepsilon$-spanned plane tree $K$ is $10\varepsilon$-narrow.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search for the narrowness assertions about plane trees with no ε-triods and ε-spanned plane trees did not return any source confirming a proof, disproof, or partial resolution. No follow-up paper resolving these two narrowness conjectures could be located, so the current status is unknown from available public sources.
